Cost -Optimized LLM Architecture for PDF -Centric Applications
This document explains techniques used to reduce LLM cost, latency, and token usage while
maintaining answer quality in a PDF -based AI system (similar to Notebook LM).
1. Context Caching – Cache the Static PDF Context
Priority: High
What it is
Context caching stores pre-processed, cleaned, and chunked PDF content so that it is not
re-sent to the LLM repeatedly for every query.
Why it matters
PDFs are usually static. Sending the same content again and again wastes tokens and increases
cost.
How it works
• Preprocess the PDF once
• Cache:
o Cleaned text
o Chunked sections
o Embeddings
• Reuse cached context for subsequent queries
Example
User uploads a 200 -page policy document:
• Bad: Send all 200 pages on every question
• Good: Cache the processed chunks and reuse them
2. Smart Model Routing – Different Models for Different Tasks
Priority: High
What it is
Use different LLMs based on task complexity , instead of sending everything to an expensive
model.
Why it matters
Not all tasks need a powerful model.
Example Routing Strategy

Task Model
PDF cleaning Llama local
Query rewrite GPT-4o Mini
Intent classification Gemini Flash
Final answer generation GPT-4o Mini
Metadata extraction Cheap local model
Example
User asks: “Summarize section 3”
→ No need for GPT -4 level reasoning
→ Route to GPT -4o Mini
3. Prompt / PDF Compression
Priority: High
What it is
Remove non-semantic noise from PDFs before sending them to the LLM.
What to remove
• Headers & footers
• Page numbers
• Repeated watermarks
• References (if not needed)
• Legal boilerplate
Why it matters
These tokens add zero reasoning value .
Example
Before cleaning
– Company XYZ
---------------------------
Section 4.2 Performance Metrics
After cleaning

4. Progressive Disclosure – Avoid Wasting Tokens
Priority: High
What it is
Only send deep context when the question requires it .
Strategy
• Start with minimal context
• Expand context only if the user asks follow -ups
Example
User: “What is this document about?”
→ Send title + abstract only
User: “Explain the training methodology”
→ Retrieve detailed sections
5. Session Memory Pruning
Priority: Medium
What it is
Periodically summarize and compress chat history instead of keeping raw messages.
Why it matters
Long chats = high token usage.
Example
After 15 messages:
Summary:
User is analysing PDF X.
They are focused on section 5 and want concise explanations.
Replace raw history with summary.
6. Output Length Control
Priority: High
What it is
Explicitly control how long and how detailed responses are .
Techniques
• max_tokens
• Bullet -point answers

• Structured formats
Example Prompt
Answer in 5 bullet points.
Max 120 words.
No explanations unless asked.
7. Cheap Models for Preprocessing
Priority: Medium
What it is
Use low-cost or local models for tasks that don’t require deep reasoning.
Tasks suitable for cheap models
• Text cleaning
• Chunking
• Metadata tagging
• Keyword extraction
Benefit
Reduces usage of expensive LLM calls.
8. Embeddings as a Cost Guardrail
Priority: High
What it is
Use embeddings to retrieve only relevant PDF sections , instead of sending the entire
document.
Workflow
1. Generate embeddings for PDF chunks
2. Store in vector DB
3. On user query:
o Embed query
o Retrieve top -K relevant chunks
4. Send only those chunks to LLM
Example

PDF = 500 pages
User asks: “Explain risk factors”
→ Retrieve only 3 –5 relevant sections
9. Caching Answers for Repeated Questions
Priority: Medium
What it is
Cache LLM responses for identical or near -identical queries .
Example
User asks:
• “What is section 2 about?”
• Another user asks the same
→ Serve cached answer instead of re -calling LLM
10. Rate Limits + Debounce
Priority: Low
What it is
Prevent accidental multiple LLM calls .
Techniques
• Button debounce
• API rate limiting
• Disable submit during streaming
Example
User presses Enter 5 times
→ Only one request is processed
Reducing Input Tokens Sent to LLM
1. Clean the PDF Aggressively
Remove all non -semantic content before chunking.
2. Merge Processing Chunks Properly
Avoid sending overlapping or duplicate content unnecessarily.
3. Use Context Caching
Reuse processed context across sessions.

4. Prune Chat History
Summarize older messages.
5. Don’t Send PDF for Simple Questions
Example:
“What does this app do?”
→ No PDF needed.
6. Remove System Prompt Bloat
Avoid long, repetitive system instructions.
Reducing Output Tokens from LLM
1. Set Output Limits
Use max_tokens.
2. Force Structured Responses
Tables, bullet points, JSON.
3. Stop Over -Explaining by Default
Only expand if user asks.
4. Stop Early
Once the question is answered, terminate generation.
Preprocessing Techniques
Cleaning the Document
Removes noise and redundancy.
Semantic Chunking
Chunks based on meaning , not fixed size.
Overlapping Chunks
Ensures context continuity across boundaries.
Metadata Enrichment
Add:
• Page number
• Section title
• Document ID
Normalize Format
Consistent casing, spacing, bullet styles.

Retrieval Stage Techniques
Hybrid Retrieval
Combine:
• Keyword search (BM25)
• Semantic embeddings
Re-ranking
Use a small model to rank retrieved chunks by relevance.
Intermediate Agents (Cheap & Fast Models)
Query Rewriter
Improves poorly phrased queries.
Intent Classifier
Detects:
• Summary
• Fact lookup
• Comparison
Scope Narrowing Agent
Limits retrieval to relevant sections only.
Context Selection Agent
Chooses best chunks to send to LLM.
Prompt Optimizer
Removes unnecessary instructions.
Routing Agent
Chooses which model to call.
Prompt Construction Techniques
Explicit Grounding
Answer only using provided context.
Structured Answers
Bullet points, tables, JSON.
Cite Sources
Include section or page references.
End-to-End System Flow

PDF Upload
↓
Preprocessing
- Cleaning
- Semantic chunking
- Metadata
↓
Vector Database
↓
User Query
↓
Intermediate Agents
- Rewrite
- Intent classify
- Narrow scope
↓
Hybrid Retrieval + Re -ranking
↓
Context Selection
↓
Final LLM Generation
Nice -to-Have Enhancements
Confidence Thresholds
Only answer if relevance score is high enough.
Evaluation Loop
Compare LLM answers with ground truth.
Asymmetric Context
Send more context for generation, less for evaluation.
Cold -Start Handling
Graceful fallback when embeddings or cache don’t exist.

Token Consumption Challenges in Business LLM Systems
Cost, Efficiency, and Optimization Report
Executive Summary
Token consumption is one of the primary cost and performance drivers in Large Language
Model (LLM) –powered business applications. Enterprises deploying AI assistants, document
chat systems, NotebookLM -style tools, and RAG platforms often experience excessi ve token
usage due to oversized context injection, inefficient retrieval strategies, verbose prompts, and
uncontrolled conversation memory.
This report identifies where tokens are most heavily consumed, why it happens, its business
impact, and the most effective optimization strategies. The goal is to enable measurable
reductions in cost, latency, and system load while improving response quali ty and scalability.
1. Why Token Efficiency Matters
Business Impact Areas
Token usage directly affects:
• API cost per request
• Infrastructure spend
• Response latency
• Throughput limits
• User experience
• System scalability
• Retry frequency
• Model routing decisions
At scale, inefficient token usage can increase operational cost by 2–5× compared to optimized
pipelines.
2. Where Maximum Tokens Are Burned
2.1 Large Context Injection (Primary Source)
Description
Systems frequently send excessive contextual data to the model, including:
• Entire PDFs
• Full knowledge base documents
• Whole policy manuals

• Large code files
• Full database exports
• Entire notebook sources
Why It Happens
• Over -cautious prompt design
• No chunk filtering
• Weak retrieval pipelines
• No context compression
• Fear of missing relevant data
Typical Token Share
45–60% of total tokens per call
2.2 Chat History Accumulation
Description
Conversation systems resend full chat history every turn.
Example Growth Pattern
Turn -based token growth:
• Turn 1 → 400 tokens
• Turn 10 → 4,000 tokens
• Turn 25 → 12,000+ tokens
Causes
• No memory pruning
• No rolling window
• No conversation summarization
• No session compression
Typical Token Share
15–25%
2.3 Inefficient RAG Retrieval
Description
Retrieval systems return too many chunks or low -relevance chunks.
Example
Instead of:
• Top 3 chunks

System sends:
• Top 12 –20 chunks
Causes
• High top -k default
• No reranking
• No similarity threshold
• No deduplication
• No semantic filtering
Typical Token Share
10–20%
2.4 Overly Long System Prompts
Description
Repeated verbose instructions in every request:
• Style rules
• Safety instructions
• Formatting guides
• Multi -rule behavior specs
Causes
• Prompt overengineering
• No prompt templating
• No server -side prompt caching
Typical Token Share
5–10%
2.5 Regeneration & Retry Loops
Description
Poor outputs trigger automatic retries or user regenerations.
Causes
• Weak prompts
• No output schema
• No temperature control
• No structured constraints
• No guardrail validation

Impact
Token cost multiplies per retry.
Typical Token Share
5–12%
2.6 Verbose Output Generation
Description
Model generates unnecessarily long answers.
Examples:
• Essay responses to short questions
• Over -detailed explanations
• Long markdown formatting
• Redundant reasoning text
Causes
• No output token limits
• No format constraints
• No brevity instructions
Typical Token Share
5–15%
2.7 Raw Data Injection
Description
Systems send unfiltered raw data:
• Logs
• JSON payloads
• Tables
• API responses
• Full transcripts
Instead of summarized or structured extracts.
2.8 Multi -Stage LLM Pipelines
Description
Pipelines with multiple chained model calls:
• Extract

• Summarize
• Reformat
• Validate
• Expand
• Generate final output
Risk
No token budgeting across stages leads to runaway cost.
3. Token Burn by Feature Type
NotebookLM -Style Systems (High Risk Areas)
Highest token burn occurs in:
• PDF chat context injection
• Studio features (mind maps, reports, slides)
• Multi -document analysis
• Conversation history
• Feature regeneration
• Multi -format outputs
4. Observability Metrics Businesses Should Track
To control token usage, systems must log:
Per Request Metrics
• input_tokens
• output_tokens
• total_tokens
• model_used
• feature_name
• response_latency
Retrieval Metrics
• chunks_retrieved
• chunk_token_count
• relevance_score_avg
Conversation Metrics
• chat_history_tokens
• memory_summary_tokens

• session_token_total
Quality Metrics
• regenerate_count
• retry_count
• failure_rate
Cost Metrics
• cost_per_call
• cost_per_user_session
• cost_per_feature
5. High -Impact Optimization Strategies
5.1 Context Compression
Remove:
• headers
• footers
• page numbers
• references
• repeated boilerplate
Savings: 20 –40%
5.2 Smart RAG Retrieval
Implement:
• top-k = 3 –5
• reranking layer
• similarity threshold
• semantic deduplication
• chunk merging
Savings: 30 –60%
5.3 Chat Memory Summarization
Strategy:
• Summarize every N turns
• Replace history with summary
• Keep only recent window

Savings: 50 –80% over long sessions
5.4 Output Length Control
Use constraints:
• max_tokens
• bullet format
• short answer mode
• structured schema outputs
Savings: 30 –70% output tokens
5.5 Prompt Minimization
Improvements:
• Prompt templates
• Remove repeated rules
• Server -side static prompts
• Short instruction sets
Savings: 200 –800 tokens per call
5.6 Context Caching
Cache:
• document embeddings
• static instructions
• document summaries
• frequently retrieved chunks
Major scale savings
5.7 Model Routing
Use:
• Small model → extraction/classification
• Medium model → summarization
• Large model → reasoning/generation
Cost reduction: 40 –70%
5.8 Token Budgeting Per Feature

Define limits:
• chat answer → 300 tokens
• summary → 500 tokens
• report → 1200 tokens
• quiz → 250 tokens
Prevents runaway responses.
6. Recommended Implementation Roadmap
Phase 1 — Measurement
• Add token logging
• Add cost tracking
• Add regenerate tracking
Phase 2 — Retrieval Optimization
• Reduce chunk count
• Add reranking
• Apply thresholds
Phase 3 — Memory Optimization
• Add chat summarization
• Rolling context window
Phase 4 — Prompt Optimization
• Template prompts
• Reduce instruction size
Phase 5 — Output Control
• Add token limits
• Enforce output schemas
Phase 6 — Model Routing
• Route tasks by complexity
7. Expected Business Outcomes
After optimization:
• 35–65% token reduction
• Lower API costs
• Faster response times
• Fewer retries

• Better answer relevance
• Higher concurrency capacity
• Improved user experience
Conclusion
Token inefficiency is the largest hidden cost driver in enterprise LLM systems. Most token
waste originates from oversized context, unfiltered retrieval, long chat histories, and verbose
prompts. With proper observability, retrieval tuning, memory compress ion, and model routing,
businesses can significantly reduce cost and improve performance while maintaining or
improving output quality.

These give maximum control and optimization ability.

Best for multi -agent workflows and conditional routing.

• Only relevant context passed

• Tool calls replace long generation

• Student query routing

Enterprise -grade planner + function orchestration.

• Modular prompts

3. RAG -Focused Orchestration Platforms
Optimized for document systems.
LlamaIndex
Document AI orchestration layer.
Strengths:

• Context compression

• Auto chunk merging

• Compressed context
• Smart chunk selection
• Query transformation
Best Fit For This Project:

• Multi -doc reasoning

End-to-end RAG platform.
Strengths:
• Neural reranking

4. Observability & Token Control Tools
These reduce waste rather than orchestrate logic.

Systems frequently send excessive contextual data to the model, including:  
• Entire PDFs  
• Full knowledge base documents  
• Whole policy manuals

• Large code files  
• Full database exports  
• Entire notebook sources  
Why It Happens  
• Over -cautious prompt design  
• No chunk filtering  
• Weak retrieval pipelines  
• No context compression  
• Fear of missing relevant data  
Typical Token Share  
45–60% of total tokens per call  
 
2.2 Chat History Accumulation  
Description  
Conversation systems resend full chat history every turn.  
Example Growth Pattern  
Turn -based token growth:  
• Turn 1 → 400 tokens  
• Turn 10 → 4,000 tokens  
• Turn 25 → 12,000+ tokens  
Causes  
• No memory pruning  
• No rolling window  
• No conversation summarization  
• No session compression  
Typical Token Share  
15–25%  
 
2.3 Inefficient RAG Retrieval  
Description  
Retrieval systems return too many chunks or low -relevance chunks.  
Example  
Instead of:  
• Top 3 chunks

System sends:  
• Top 12 –20 chunks  
Causes  
• High top -k default  
• No reranking  
• No similarity threshold  
• No deduplication  
• No semantic filtering  
Typical Token Share  
10–20%  
 
2.4 Overly Long System Prompts  
Description  
Repeated verbose instructions in every request:  
• Style rules  
• Safety instructions  
• Formatting guides  
• Multi -rule behavior specs  
Causes  
• Prompt overengineering  
• No prompt templating  
• No server -side prompt caching  
Typical Token Share  
5–10%  
 
2.5 Regeneration & Retry Loops  
Description  
Poor outputs trigger automatic retries or user regenerations.  
Causes  
• Weak prompts  
• No output schema  
• No temperature control  
• No structured constraints  
• No guardrail validation

Impact  
Token cost multiplies per retry.  
Typical Token Share  
5–12%  
 
2.6 Verbose Output Generation  
Description  
Model generates unnecessarily long answers.  
Examples:  
• Essay responses to short questions  
• Over -detailed explanations  
• Long markdown formatting  
• Redundant reasoning text  
Causes  
• No output token limits  
• No format constraints  
• No brevity instructions  
Typical Token Share  
5–15%  
 
2.7 Raw Data Injection  
Description  
Systems send unfiltered raw data:  
• Logs  
• JSON payloads  
• Tables  
• API responses  
• Full transcripts  
Instead of summarized or structured extracts.  
 
2.8 Multi -Stage LLM Pipelines  
Description  
Pipelines with multiple chained model calls:  
• Extract

• Summarize  
• Reformat  
• Validate  
• Expand  
• Generate final output  
Risk  
No token budgeting across stages leads to runaway cost.

5. High -Impact Optimization Strategies  
5.1 Context Compression  
Remove:  
• headers  
• footers  
• page numbers  
• references  
• repeated boilerplate  
Savings: 20 –40%  
 
5.2 Smart RAG Retrieval  
Implement:  
• top-k = 3 –5 
• reranking layer  
• similarity threshold  
• semantic deduplication  
• chunk merging  
Savings: 30 –60%  
 
5.3 Chat Memory Summarization  
Strategy:  
• Summarize every N turns  
• Replace history with summary  
• Keep only recent window

Savings: 50 –80% over long sessions  
 
5.4 Output Length Control  
Use constraints:  
• max_tokens  
• bullet format  
• short answer mode  
• structured schema outputs  
Savings: 30 –70% output tokens  
 
5.5 Prompt Minimization  
Improvements:  
• Prompt templates  
• Remove repeated rules  
• Server -side static prompts  
• Short instruction sets  
Savings: 200 –800 tokens per call  
 
5.6 Context Caching  
Cache:  
• document embeddings  
• static instructions  
• document summaries  
• frequently retrieved chunks  
Major scale savings  
 
5.7 Model Routing  
Use: 
• Small model → extraction/classification  
• Medium model → summarization  
• Large model → reasoning/generation  
Cost reduction: 40 –70%  
 
5.8 Token Budgeting Per Feature

Define limits:  
• chat answer → 300 tokens  
• summary → 500 tokens  
• report → 1200 tokens  
• quiz → 250 tokens  
Prevents runaway responses.

Conclusion  
Token inefficiency is the largest hidden cost driver in enterprise LLM systems. Most token 
waste originates from oversized context, unfiltered retrieval, long chat histories, and verbose 
prompts. With proper observability, retrieval tuning, memory compress ion, and model routing, 
businesses can significantly reduce cost and improve performance while maintaining or 
improving output quality.
